newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN GOVERNMENT COMMUNICATES POORLY-MONITOR.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN GOVERNMENT COMMUNICATES POORLY-MONITOR.

text.p: South Africa trailed the rest of the world in communicating government achievements and policies to the people and to potential investors abroad, a task group on communications warned on Wednesday.
"We fall as a country far behind other countries in the importance we attach to communication," respected former editor Raymond Louw told parliament's committee on communications.
Louw is a member of a task group appointed by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki to investigate government communication and the ownership and control of the country's media.
Louw said South Africa had failed to emulate countries like the United States in advertising its policies to potential investors abroad.
"Nationally, at best, our communications are in disarray," he said.
Louw said South Africa had developed a reasonable infrastructure to inform a section of society, but had done nothing to communicate with the majority.
Mandla Langa, another member of the group, said in the interim report to parliament that the ownership of South Africa's media remained heavily skewed towards whites.

"We cannot by any stretch of the imagination say that there is comprehensive diversity in the media.... By and large the impression is that government is not reaching those parts of the community it is supposed to reach. It's as simple as that," he said.

The task group made its report a few hours before Anglo American Corp of South Africa announced an agreement to sell 20 percent of the industrial holding company Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd to the National Empowerment Consortium (NEC), which represents black investors.
Johnnies controls the Times Media Ltd publishing group, whose titles include Business Day, the Financial Mail and the Sunday Times.
